name: Scroll Reveal Section
summary: A panel grid that animates from its own scroll position using native CSS scroll-driven animation. Zero JavaScript, zero observers.

attempts.prompt: Make a section where cards fade in as you scroll to them.
attempts.problem: Reached straight for IntersectionObserver and a .is-visible class. That ships JavaScript for something the browser now does natively, and it hides every card behind opacity 0 in CSS. If the script fails to load or is blocked, the entire section is permanently invisible, and the content is gone for anyone without JS.

attempts.prompt: Do it with CSS scroll-driven animations instead of IntersectionObserver.
attempts.problem: Used animation-timeline: view() correctly but applied the keyframes unconditionally. In a browser without support the cards inherited the from state and stayed at opacity 0 forever. It also ignored prefers-reduced-motion, so the section moved for users who had asked the system for no motion.

finalPrompt:
Build a scroll-reveal section in plain HTML and CSS with no JavaScript at all.

Use native CSS scroll-driven animation: animation-timeline: view() with an animation-range of roughly entry 10% to cover 34%, so each card animates against its own position in the viewport rather than the page's scroll offset. Do not use IntersectionObserver, scroll listeners, or any script.

The fallback behaviour is the part that matters most. Wrap the animation in @supports (animation-timeline: view()) so that a browser without support never applies the keyframes at all, and the cards render fully visible by default. The content must never be hidden by CSS that only a supported browser can undo. Assume the animation will not run and make sure the section still reads correctly.

Nest a prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference media query inside that @supports block, so reduced motion means no animation rather than a shorter one.

Markup: a section with a heading and a short lead, then an ordered list of four cards, each with a monospace index number, a title and a line of body text. Use semantic elements, real heading levels, and an ol because the cards are numbered.

The grid is repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) so it reflows from four columns to one without a single media query.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--surface), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), var(--raised), var(--radius), var(--mono). No literal hex, rgb or hsl anywhere.
why:
Two lessons sit in this one, and both are about what happens when the happy path does not run.

The first is that asking for an effect gets you the most familiar implementation of that effect, not the best one. "Fade in on scroll" has meant IntersectionObserver for years, so that is the default answer. Naming the modern API explicitly is the only reliable way past it.

The second is the more valuable one. Scroll-driven animation has an ugly failure mode: the keyframes hide the content, and an unsupported browser never unhides it. Saying "add a fallback" is too vague to fix this — it produces a fallback for the animation, not for the content. What worked was stating the invariant directly: assume the animation will not run, and the section must still read correctly. That single sentence forced the @supports wrapper into the right place, around the animation rather than around the visibility.

Write the constraint as a property the result must hold, not as a feature to add.
